clue.text: Reckless villain can show solicitude

parts.note: a villain is a devil of a man
may and can both express permission
to show solicitude is to care

explanation.surface: A wicked rogue turns out to be surprisingly caring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'show solicitude' is a verb phrase, matched by the verb CARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone heedless of consequences has a carefree, devil-take-it attitude, so the hyphenated phrase is an adjective for rashness.

clue.text: Pearly queen's lesser, domestic, rank

parts.note: a pearly queen is a London costermonger's ceremonial queen; in Cockney speech a man calls his wife his 'old dutch', so the domestic title just below a queen is the noblewoman's rank used for a wife

explanation.surface: Ranking the costermongers' royalty, below the Pearly Queen herself.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are London street traders in button-covered costumes; Cockney 'my old dutch' (short for this title) means 'my wife', so the domestic rank is one step below queen.
explanation.definitionFit: In the peerage the title ranks just beneath royalty, and in Cockney slang it names a man's wife at home.

clue.text: Britain somehow drops two after six — how thrilling!

indicators.note: the shuffled letters come after the six

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: somehow says the remaining letters are arranged in some other way
drops says the named letters fall out of the word Britain

parts.note: II is two in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An excited exclamation about Britain losing a couple of wickets after reaching six.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two' is the Roman II, the two I's that 'drops' takes out, leaving BRTAN, which the anagram signal rearranges into BRANT; the surface reads like cricket, but 'six' is just VI.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vibrant pulses with energy, so it is exciting or stirring.

clue.text: Obedient friends, Romans, countrymen

parts.note: Mark Antony's speech in Julius Caesar opens by asking friends, Romans and countrymen to lend him their ears; those who obey are the people who do so

explanation.surface: Mark Antony's famous crowd, pictured as a docile audience doing as asked.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Shakespeare's 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears': the obedient ones lend their ears, so they are the audience.
explanation.definitionFit: People who lend their ears are an audience paying attention, which is what this crowd becomes.

clue.text: Forty winks wouldn't half put him to sleep

definitions.text: Forty winks wouldn't half put him to sleep

parts.words: Forty winks wouldn't half put him to sleep
parts.note: the Greek giant of myth had a hundred eyes, so forty eyes closing would not even send half of them to sleep

explanation.surface: Someone so restless that a short nap could never knock him out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forty winks' is a nap, but here it is counted literally: forty closed eyes out of the mythical watchman's hundred is under half.
explanation.definitionFit: The hundred-eyed watchman of Greek myth, set by Hera to guard Io, always kept some eyes open.

clue.text: Equine accuser

definitions.meaning: a war horse ridden into battle
one who brings a charge against someone

explanation.definitionFit: A cavalry mount is a war horse, and a person who brings a criminal charge is, literally, one who charges.

clue.text: This animal ran about 200 circuits.

indicators.note: about says the word ran goes round the other letters

parts.note: taken as written
CC is 200 in Roman numerals
two rings, each shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: An athletic creature that ran some two hundred laps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circuits' gives two O's because each lap is a ring. The trailing dots carry 'This animal' on into 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A masked North American mammal is the creature the clue points to.

clue.text: … and this extended St Augustine's see

definitions.text: and this extended St Augustine's see

parts.words: and this extended St Augustine's see
parts.note: St Augustine was Bishop of Hippo in North Africa; that city's name, extended to full length, is the river horse's full name, continuing the 'This animal' of 6 down

explanation.surface: Continuing the animal theme with a note on a famous saint's bishopric.
explanation.walkthrough: Augustine's see was Hippo, in what is now Algeria. 'Hippo' is also the short form of the animal's name, so the extended form is the full name.
explanation.definitionFit: The full name of the large African river animal is what the short form 'hippo' abbreviates.

clue.text: Copper takes transport in the first place to get nocturnal oppressor

indicators.note: the first place says the little word goes at the front of the rest

parts.note: taken as written
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a bus is public transport

explanation.surface: A policeman catching a bus to reach a midnight tormentor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the chemical symbol CU; 'takes' joins it to BUS, and 'in the first place' puts IN at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A demon thought to lie on sleepers was blamed for nightmares, so it oppresses people by night.

clue.text: Cast an eye, so it ricocheted?

definitions.meaning: bounced off at an angle, as a stray bullet does

explanation.definitionFit: Taking a quick look and a shot bouncing off a surface are both described by the same past-tense verb.

clue.text: Strife growing from them may be strong and heated

indicators.note: may be says these words could become something else once rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A suggestion that arguments arise from strong, heated words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' signals an anagram of STRONG and HEATED; 'and' only links. In Greek myth Cadmus sowed the teeth of a slain serpent, and armed men sprang up and fought one another.
explanation.definitionFit: Myth tells of serpent's teeth sown in the ground that grew into warring soldiers, so they stand for things that breed conflict.

clue.text: Lords always taken in by an attendant

indicators.note: taken in by says the first piece is held inside the second

parts.note: a page is a boy attendant
e'er, poetic for ever, means always

explanation.surface: Members of the upper house kept forever in the care of a servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in by' signals a container; 'always' gives the poetic contraction e'er, as in 'for e'er'.
explanation.definitionFit: The nobility collectively, those entitled to sit in the House of Lords, make up this body.

clue.text: So a ring changes a girl's status in Italy

indicators.note: changes says these letters swap round into a new order

explanation.surface: Marriage, sealed with a ring, alters an Italian woman's title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges SO A RING. The surface works too: a wedding ring turns an Italian signorina into a married woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian title for a married woman, equivalent to Mrs or madam, marks the status a wedding brings.

clue.text: Assume a situation without one

parts.note: to put forward a state of affairs as a premise when no such state of affairs actually exists yet

explanation.surface: Imagining circumstances that aren't really there.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb means to suppose something for the sake of argument: you assume a situation even without having one.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something down as a premise is to postulate it, assuming it is so for argument's sake.

clue.text: Monoglot optimist?

parts.note: the invented world language takes its name from a word meaning 'one who hopes', so a speaker of a single universal tongue is pictured as a hopeful person

explanation.surface: A cheerful person who speaks just one language.
explanation.walkthrough: Zamenhof published his international language under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes', and the name stuck to the language.
explanation.definitionFit: Its name means 'hoping one', and it was designed as one shared language for everyone.

clue.text: Go by without putting in anywhere ? Then you won't need them

definitions.text: Go by without putting in anywhere ? Then you won't need them

parts.words: Go by without putting in anywhere ? Then you won't need them
parts.note: if a ship sails past every harbour without calling, no border control is passed, so travel documents are unnecessary; the opening also reads as 'go by' plus 'harbours'

explanation.surface: Travel advice: if you never stop at a harbour, you can leave your papers at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The first words split as PASS (go by) and PORTS (places to put in): you only need these documents if you put in at ports rather than pass them.
explanation.definitionFit: Travel documents are shown at frontier posts and harbours, so a voyage calling nowhere needs none.

clue.text: Plants a French husband in jobs

indicators.note: in says the husband is placed inside the word for jobs

parts.note: tasks are jobs
mari is French for husband

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's husband placed among gardening chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals a container; 'a French husband' is one phrase for the French word, so 'a' gives no letter of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: These feathery shrubs that grow by the sea are a kind of plant.

clue.text: He contrives to control business

parts.note: one who manages, in the sense of contriving or getting by, and also the person running a business

explanation.surface: A schemer angling to take over a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manage' means both 'contrive' (as in 'we'll manage') and 'run'; the person described does both.
explanation.definitionFit: The person running a firm or department directs its affairs, and to manage is also to contrive.

clue.text: Flower swindle upset no one

parts.note: a ramp is British slang for a swindle

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the words no and one upside down, reading them bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A con involving a flower leaves nobody upset.
explanation.walkthrough: RAMP is British slang for a racket or swindle. 'upset' reverses NO + I to give ION.
explanation.definitionFit: This blue bellflower, once grown for its edible root, is a wildflower.

clue.text: Order form

definitions.meaning: a rank or category in a classification
a group of pupils taught together in a British school

explanation.definitionFit: A taxonomic category and a school year group are both named by the same word.

clue.text: Have a good loaf in this hospital

definitions.text: Have a good loaf in this hospital

parts.words: Have a good loaf in this hospital
parts.note: a loaf of two stacked rounds and a small country hospital share the same descriptive name, and 'loaf' also means laze about

explanation.surface: A patient taking it easy on a ward.
explanation.walkthrough: A cottage loaf is a British bread of two round tiers; a cottage hospital is a small rural hospital. 'Loaf' also means to idle, as a patient might.
explanation.definitionFit: Small village houses give their name both to a two-tiered loaf and to a small rural hospital.

clue.text: Photo record has points on primary chicken-feed

parts.note: a photo album records pictures
E and N are compass points

explanation.surface: A snapshot book with tips about basic poultry feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'on' only link. The definition is fair: egg white is the first food the developing chick draws on.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg white nourishes the embryo inside the shell, so it is a chick's very first food.

clue.text: Free degree. Numbers take it

parts.note: MA, Master of Arts, is a university degree
Num is the abbreviation for the Book of Numbers in the Bible
taken as written

explanation.surface: A free qualification that statistics can win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' only links; Numbers is the Old Testament book, abbreviated NUM.
explanation.definitionFit: To release a slave from bondage is to set them at liberty, the verb sense here.

clue.text: Herb signifies "I am yours"?

parts.note: the herb's name splits into old forms meaning 'yours' and 'myself', so it seems to declare that I belong to you

explanation.surface: A love token in the language of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the herb's name into THY + ME: 'thy' is old English for 'your', so it says 'me, yours'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small aromatic kitchen herb used in stuffings fits the picture.

clue.text: River board says "O.K. for drinking"

parts.note: the Po is the great river of northern Italy
a table is a board, as in 'board and lodging'

explanation.surface: A water authority declares the supply safe to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'says' only links; a 'River board' was a British water authority, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that is safe to drink is described with this formal adjective.

clue.text: Mean gesture by one deflated fairy

parts.note: a sign is a gesture
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: deflated says the word fairy has its air let out

explanation.surface: A spiteful gesture made beside a fairy that has gone flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deflated' removes AIR from FAIRY, leaving FY. 'Mean' looks like an adjective (stingy) but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean something is to indicate or denote it, a synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Repeat confession when let in again

definitions.meaning: to confess or own up a second time

explanation.definitionFit: Owning up once more and allowing back in are both the verb formed by putting 're-' before a word for confess or allow entry.

clue.text: Monster sales not patronized by this do-it-yourself expert

definitions.text: Monster sales not patronized by this do-it-yourself expert

parts.words: Monster sales not patronized by this do-it-yourself expert
parts.note: Mary Shelley's scientist built his creature himself from parts rather than buying one, so he never shopped at a monster sale

explanation.surface: A handyman who shuns the big bargain sales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monster sales' reads as huge sales, but means sales of monsters: Shelley's scientist made his own monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Shelley's scientist assembled his creature with his own hands, a home-made monster.
